title: Tobit
subtitle: a family story of exile, a hidden angel, and alms that do not go unseen
lead: Tobit tells of a devout Israelite of the tribe of Naphtali, carried off to Nineveh by the Assyrians, who feeds the hungry and buries the dead even when the king forbids it. He goes blind. On the same day, far away in Ecbatana in Media, a young woman named Sarah prays for death, because a demon, Asmodeus, has killed each of her seven husbands on the wedding night. God hears both prayers and sends the angel Raphael, disguised as a kinsman named Azariah, to guide Tobit's son Tobias on a journey east. On the way a fish, a wedding and a homecoming set everything right. The book ends with Raphael revealing who he is, Tobit's hymn to a rebuilt Jerusalem, and his last words to his family. It has 14 chapters and 245 verses.

Who reads it as Scripture. The Catholic Church and the Orthodox churches (Eastern and Oriental, including the Ethiopian) include Tobit in their Old Testament; Catholics call it deuterocanonical, "of the second canon." Protestants place it among the Apocrypha: Lutheran and Anglican Bibles long printed it between the Testaments to be read for example of life, but not to set doctrine, and Reformed and Baptist confessions give it no authority. It is not in the Jewish Bible, though Jews copied it in Aramaic and Hebrew at Qumran. Most scholars read it as an edifying Jewish story written around 225–175 BC, probably in Aramaic, and set in the Assyrian exile of the 700s BC.
facts: The Catholic Church (defined at Trent, 1546), the Eastern Orthodox churches, the Oriental Orthodox churches and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Among the Apocrypha for Lutherans and Anglicans (read, not used for doctrine). Not Scripture for Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches, or for Judaism.

Unknown. The book speaks in Tobit's voice in 1:3–3:6 and then in the third person, and has Raphael tell Tobit and Tobias to write everything down (12:20). Older Catholic and Orthodox tradition took Tobit and Tobias as its writers; most scholars think an unknown Jewish writer composed it long after the events it describes.
Most scholars: about 225–175 BC (Fitzmyer); some say as early as 300 BC. It shows no knowledge of the persecution of Antiochus IV (167 BC), and the oldest copies are from about 100 BC.
Nineveh in Assyria and Ecbatana and Rages in Media, in the reigns of Shalmaneser, Sennacherib and Esarhaddon (about 730–670 BC), with a last look ahead to the fall of Nineveh (612 BC)
Unknown: the eastern Jewish exile, Judea and Egypt have all been proposed
Probably Aramaic (four Aramaic copies at Qumran); a Hebrew copy was found too, and a few scholars think Hebrew came first

Aramaic and Hebrew fragments from Qumran (about 100 BC to the turn of the era); two main Greek forms, the longer in Codex Sinaiticus and the shorter in Vaticanus and Alexandrinus (300s–400s AD); Old Latin; Jerome's Latin Vulgate; Syriac, Coptic, Armenian and Ethiopic translations; medieval Hebrew and Aramaic retellings
A short story or novella of a family, with prayers, a testament of moral advice (4; 14), an angel's revelation (12) and a hymn (13)
authorship: For many centuries Catholic and Orthodox readers took the book as a true account written down by Tobit and his son. Tobit speaks in the first person in 1:3–3:6, and Raphael commands them to write what happened (12:20). In Jerome's Latin, the Catholic text for centuries, the whole book is told in the third person, and the angel tells them to make known all God's wonders (Vulgate 12:20). Walter Drum's article in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1912) still defended the book's history, explaining the hard points one by one, for example by reading the Greek "Enemessar" as Sargon II. Some Catholic and Orthodox readers still hold that view.

Most scholars, including most Catholic and Orthodox scholars today, read Tobit as an edifying story by an unknown Jewish writer of about 225–175 BC. The writer knew the Torah, the Prophets and wisdom books well, and also the Aramaic tale of Ahiqar, which he weaves in by making Ahiqar Tobit's nephew (1:21–22). The many problems of history and geography (see "How reliable is it?") suggest a writer living centuries later and far from Assyria, telling a story about the past to teach his own time. Fitzmyer and Moore, both Catholic scholars, take this view.

Scholars disagree. Some think of the eastern exile (Mesopotamia or Persia), because the story is set there and treats life among Gentiles as normal. Others think of Judea, because the writer gets eastern geography wrong and centers his hope on Jerusalem (13:9–18; 14:5). Egypt has also been suggested, because the demon flees there (8:3) and the book was popular among Greek-speaking Jews. Most say the question cannot be settled.

audience.to: Jews living as a minority among Gentiles in the 200s BC, under Greek kings (the Ptolemies of Egypt and then the Seleucids of Syria), whether in the eastern exile or in a Judea that felt itself still scattered. The book is set five hundred years earlier among the northern tribes taken by Assyria, but it speaks to families who had to answer daily questions: Whom may our children marry? Can we eat our neighbors' food? What do we owe the poor and the dead? Why do good people suffer? Has God forgotten the scattered tribes? Both Greek forms and the Qumran copies show that Jews in the land of Israel and in the Greek-speaking world read it.
audience.why: The writer wanted to show how to stay faithful far from the Temple, with no prophet and no miracle in sight. His answers are the practices of an ordinary Jewish household: prayer, fasting, almsgiving, honoring parents, burying the dead, marrying within the people, and keeping the food laws (1:10–11; 4:3–19; 12:8–10). His comfort is that God works unseen through those practices: the angel walking beside Tobias is never recognized until the end, and the prayers of two despairing people are heard on the same day (3:16–17). His hope is national: all Israel, the lost northern tribes too, will come home, and a splendid Jerusalem will draw the nations (13:9–18; 14:5–7). Knowing the readers changes the reading. Tobit is not mainly a book about demons and fish remedies. It is a book about how a family keeps faith in exile and trusts that God has not stopped caring.
views: Many scholars think the first readers lived in Mesopotamia or Persia, where Jewish communities had lived since the exiles of the 700s and 500s BC. The book's ease with Gentile neighbors, its business trips and bank deposits (1:14; 4:20), and its use of the Ahiqar story, popular in the Aramaic East, would fit them.

Others think the writer lived in Judea and used the story of the northern exiles to speak to all Jews who felt scattered. His hope for the Temple and Jerusalem (13:9–18; 14:5) and his mistakes about eastern geography (5:6) would fit a Judean writer.

Many read Tobit's long speeches to his son (4:3–21; 14:3–11) as family teaching in the style of Proverbs and Sirach. Parents could read them to their children, and the story would make the teaching memorable.

For the churches that read it as Scripture, the first readers include the church itself, which hears in Tobit God's care through his angels, the value of prayer and almsgiving, and a model of holy marriage (8:4–8).

outline: Title: the book of the words of Tobit of the tribe of Naphtali

The journey: the fish from the Tigris, and Raphael's plan for Tobias and Sarah
Raguel's house in Ecbatana: the marriage contract, the demon put to flight, the couple's prayer, the wedding feast
Raphael brings Gabael and the money from Rages
Tobit and Anna wait and worry; Raguel sends the couple home
Homecoming: the fish's gall heals Tobit's eyes
Raphael reveals who he is: "one of the seven angels"
Tobit's hymn of praise and his vision of a rebuilt Jerusalem
Tobit's last words and death, the warning about Nineveh, and the deaths of Tobias and his family's elders

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts Tobit among the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament, defined as Scripture at the Council of Trent (1546) after earlier lists such as Hippo (393), Carthage (397) and Florence (1442).

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches read Tobit in their Old Testament, from the Septuagint. Many Eastern Orthodox teachers call it one of the books "worthy to be read" (anagignoskomena), and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) counted it as Scripture.

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place Tobit among the Apocrypha. Lutheran and Anglican Bibles long printed it between the Testaments as good to read for example of life, but not to establish doctrine (Article VI). Reformed churches give it no authority (Westminster Confession 1.3).

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read Tobit as an edifying Jewish story written around 225–175 BC, probably in Aramaic, set in the Assyrian exile to teach faithfulness, almsgiving and trust in God's hidden care.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: Tobit is not in the Jewish Bible, but Jews copied it in Aramaic and Hebrew at Qumran, and medieval Jews retold it in Hebrew and Aramaic versions. It is a window on diaspora Jewish piety in the centuries before Jesus.

sections.b:
Read it first as a story, and enjoy it. Tobit is told with great skill: two prayers rise from two cities on the same day (3:1–17); the reader knows from 5:4 that the guide is an angel, while the characters do not; a dog trots along on the journey (6:2; 11:4); a father digs a grave for the son-in-law he expects to find dead (8:9–12); a mother scans the road every day (10:7; 11:5). Martin Luther, who did not count it as Scripture, still called it a "truly beautiful, wholesome, and useful" story. Much of its humor and warmth comes from that gap between what the characters see and what God is doing.

Then read it as teaching. The book's center is Tobit's speech to his son (4:3–21) and Raphael's speech at the end (12:6–10): prayer with fasting and alms is good, and alms rescue from death. The story shows those words coming true. Read Tobit's hymn (13) and last words (14) as the book's horizon: the exile will end, the tribes will come home, and the nations will come to Jerusalem.

Read it alongside the books it echoes: the search for a wife among kinsmen in the east (Genesis 24; Genesis 29), the righteous sufferer (Job 1–2), the faithful foreign-born wife and family loyalty (Ruth), and the warnings against Nineveh in Jonah and Nahum, which Tobit names (14:4). The notes mark where Tobit draws on the Hebrew Bible, where the New Testament may echo it, and where it goes beyond or differs from the 66 books.

The Plain English Translation is translated for this site from the Greek, as printed by H. B. Swete (1907). Tobit survives in two main Greek forms. The Plain English Translation follows the longer one, found in Codex Sinaiticus (often called GII), as most modern translations and scholars do, because the Aramaic and Hebrew fragments from Qumran agree with it. Where Sinaiticus has gaps (4:7–19 and 13:6–10, and two single verses in chapter 11), the Plain English Translation follows the shorter text of Codex Vaticanus (GI), and a variant note says so. The variant notes also report where the shorter Greek, Jerome's Latin Vulgate and the Qumran fragments (as reported by Fitzmyer) differ in ways that matter.

The King James Version's Apocrypha, which follows the shorter Greek, and the Douay-Rheims, which follows the Vulgate, were used only to check the sense. Names use the usual English forms (Tobit, Tobias, Anna, Sarah, Raguel, Edna, Gabael, Ahiqar, Raphael, Asmodeus, Nineveh, Ecbatana, Rages), with the Greek in a note the first time where it differs.

Two prayers, one answer. The book's design is a double plot. Tobit in Nineveh and Sarah in Ecbatana both reach the end of their strength and ask to die (3:6; 3:13–15). God hears both "at that very moment" and sends one angel to heal both (3:16–17). The rest of the book draws the two threads together.

Mercy and its reward. Tobit's alms and burials (1:16–18) cost him his goods and then his sight, but in the end alms "rescue from death" (4:10; 12:9; 14:10–11). The book does not say the righteous never suffer: it shows a good man suffering and a hidden God at work.

Angels and demons. Raphael (Hebrew "God heals") is unusual among the angels of Jewish writings: he travels for weeks as a human companion. Asmodeus is one of the few named demons in Jewish writings of the time. The book pictures angels who carry the memory of prayers before God (12:12–15) and a demon who can be driven off and bound (8:2–3).

Family and marriage. Honor your mother (4:3–4), marry within your father's people as the patriarchs did (4:12–13), and pray together before your wedding night (8:4–8). The couple's prayer, which recalls Genesis 2:18, is still read at many Catholic weddings.

Exile and return. Tobit is from the northern tribe of Naphtali, the "lost" tribes. The book insists that they still belong to Israel and that God will gather them (13:5; 14:5–7).

Readers who compare English Bibles are often surprised that their Tobit differs. The reason is that Tobit was copied in two main Greek forms. The shorter form (GI), in Codex Vaticanus and Codex Alexandrinus, is the one the King James Version and most older Bibles translated. The longer form (GII), in Codex Sinaiticus, is about a third longer, fuller in its details and closer to the Semitic idiom. Most scholars think GII is nearer the original and GI a smoothed, shortened version, because the Qumran fragments in Aramaic and Hebrew agree with GII where they overlap. A third Greek form (GIII) survives for 6:9–12:22 in two later manuscripts, minuscules 106 and 107, which give the shorter text for the rest of the book (Di Lella, following Hanhart). The Old Latin translation was made from a Greek text like GII.

Catholic readers have a third Tobit too. Jerome's Latin Vulgate, made from an Aramaic copy, was the Catholic Church's official text from the Middle Ages until modern times, and the Douay-Rheims Bible translates it. It differs in many places. The best known is the counsel that Tobias and Sarah spend three nights in prayer before they come together (Vulgate 6:16–22; 8:4–5), the origin of the medieval custom of the "Tobias nights."

Tobit has had a long life in Christian practice. The early church quoted its sayings about alms (Polycarp, To the Philippians 10.2, echoes 4:10 and 12:9), Cyprian drew heavily on it in his treatise On Works and Almsgiving on it, and Ambrose preached a whole sermon on it against lending at interest. Later Christian teaching added burying the dead, Tobit's own work (1:17–18; 2:3–8), to the list of the works of mercy in Matthew 25:35–36.

Catholic readers hear Tobit in the weekday readings of the Mass and at weddings, where the prayer of Tobias and Sarah (8:4–8) is one of the Old Testament readings offered. Catholics and Orthodox honor Raphael as an archangel, with Michael and Gabriel. The Church of England's Book of Common Prayer (1662) used two sayings of Tobit (4:7; 4:8–9) among the sentences read as the alms were collected. In art, "Tobias and the Angel" became a favorite subject in Renaissance Italy, often said to have been painted for families sending a son on a journey, with the boy, the angel, the fish and the little dog.

• Tobit (Greek Tōbeith in Sinaiticus, Tōbeit in Vaticanus, Tōbit in Alexandrinus) and Tobias (Tōbias), probably from Hebrew Tobiyah, "the LORD is my good." The Latin Vulgate calls both father and son Tobias.
  • Raphael, "God heals," the angel who heals Tobit's eyes and frees Sarah. He calls himself Azariah, "the LORD helps," son of Hananiah, "the LORD is gracious" (5:13).
  • Asmodeus (Greek Asmodaios, or Asmodaus in Vaticanus), the demon. Many scholars connect the name with the Persian aēšma-daēva, "demon of wrath"; others with a Hebrew root meaning "destroy."
  • Ahiqar (Greek Acheicharos or Achiacharos), Tobit's nephew, the hero of an older Aramaic tale of a wise royal official.
  • Alms (Greek eleēmosynē, "mercy, a deed of mercy"): gifts to the poor, the book's key word.
  • Ecbatana (modern Hamadan in Iran), the Median capital; Rages (Rhagae, near modern Tehran), where Tobit left his money.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a book about seeing
spec.body: Tobit's plot turns on sight. A good man is blinded by bird droppings (2:10); Raphael is sent so that he may "see God's light" (3:17); Tobias stands face to face with an angel and does not know it (5:4); Anna watches the road for her son (10:7; 11:5); the gall opens Tobit's eyes (11:11–14); and the angel's last word is that they never saw him eat but saw a vision (12:19). The book's real subject may be that God's help is present but unseen, and that faith is learning to see it. The blind father keeps trusting, and the seeing son never notices. Scholars have often noted the theme of blindness and light in Tobit; the claim that sight is the key to the whole design, with 12:19 as its climax, is my own reading.

spec.title: Claude's theory: an answer about the lost tribes
spec.body: Most of the Hebrew Bible says little about what became of the northern tribes after 722 BC. Tobit puts a man of Naphtali at its center, makes him more faithful than his tribe (1:4–8), and ends with the promise that all Israel's scattered people will come home (13:5; 14:5–7). A Judean or diaspora reader of the 200s BC might have wondered whether the northern exiles were still kin and still under God's care. The book's answer is yes: they are family, they kept the law in exile, and their story is part of Israel's. Scholars have discussed the book's "all Israel" outlook; reading the whole book as an answer to that question is my suggestion.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Luke's fish and Raphael's vision
spec.body: Raphael travels with Tobias, eats with the family, and then reveals that he ate nothing: they saw a vision (12:19). In Luke, the risen Jesus walks with two disciples who do not recognize him (Luke 24:13–31), then shows the eleven that he is not a spirit by eating a piece of fish in front of them (Luke 24:36–43). The contrast between angels who only seem to eat and the risen Jesus who really eats has been drawn by commentators on Luke, so it is not my discovery. My small addition is the fish: Tobit's story turns on a fish caught on the journey, and Luke's risen traveler proves he is no vision by eating fish. Whether Luke meant any echo of Tobit is a guess.

views: Yes. Tobit is one of the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament. It was on the lists of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) and of Pope Innocent I (405), and the Council of Florence (1442) named it. The Council of Trent (1546) defined the whole list, Tobit included, as sacred and canonical, with an anathema on anyone who rejects it. "Deuterocanonical" means received later or after debate, not less inspired.

Yes, in the Old Testament, though Orthodox teachers explain its rank in two ways. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named Tobit among the "genuine parts of Scripture." Philaret's catechism (1839), following Athanasius, counts 22 books and says the others were appointed by the Fathers to be read by those preparing for baptism. Kallistos Ware writes that most Orthodox scholars today hold these books are part of the Bible but stand on a lower footing.

Yes, by long use. The Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches read Tobit in their Old Testament, in translations made from the Greek. They have held no council like Trent to define the list; their Bibles, lectionaries and teaching (for example a Coptic diocese's page on the deuterocanonical books) are the evidence.
Yes. Tobit is among the Old Testament books of the 81-book Bible of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches, in Ge'ez, in both ways of counting that canon.

Not Scripture, but good to read. Luther's Bible of 1534 put Tobit with the Apocrypha between the Testaments, as books not held equal to Holy Scripture yet useful and good to read. His preface to Tobit says it is fine history if the events happened, and a beautiful, useful drama if they did not. Lutheran confessions never fixed the canon; Martin Chemnitz taught that such books may not be used to prove doctrine.

Not canonical, but read. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lists "the Book of Tobias" among the books that "the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine," quoting Jerome. The Prayer Book read Tobit in its lessons and used two of its sayings at the offering, and the Homily of Alms Deeds, which Article XXXV commends, quotes Tobit's counsel on alms with the words "The same lesson doth the Holy Ghost also teach in sundry places of the Scripture."

No. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture," and are to be used only as other human writings. The Belgic Confession (article 6) allows them to be read for instruction where they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm any point of faith. Reformed writers such as Archibald Alexander argued that Tobit's angel tells a falsehood and that its fish remedies are fabulous.

No, but it is honored. Anabaptists denied the Apocrypha divine inspiration, as the Reformers did, yet esteemed Tobit, and Old Order Amish weddings traditionally base the sermon on it, as the Mennonite Encyclopedia reports.
No. John Wesley's Articles of Religion (1784) kept the Anglican list of canonical books but left out the paragraph that names the Apocrypha, so Tobit has no place in Methodist doctrine.

No. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) nearly repeats Westminster: the Apocrypha are no part of the canon and have no authority in the church. Most Baptists and other evangelicals hold the 66-book Bible and read Tobit, if at all, as Jewish background to the New Testament.

traditions.q: May Tobit be used to establish doctrine?
views: Yes. Trent received all the listed books "with an equal affection of piety and reverence" and said these are the witnesses the council would use in confirming doctrine and restoring morals. The Catechism cites Tobit, alongside other books, on almsgiving and on marriage.

Yes, within the church's tradition, but with care. The Orthodox read Tobit in worship and draw moral and spiritual teaching from it; many Orthodox theologians, following Athanasius and Jerome, give these books less weight than the Hebrew canon when deciding doctrine. There is no single ruling.

Yes, as part of the Old Testament the church reads, though these churches have issued no ruling that singles the deuterocanonical books out, and their teaching uses Tobit mainly for prayer, alms and marriage.
Yes. The Ethiopian and Eritrean churches make no distinction of rank within their 81-book Bible in the sources known to us, so Tobit may be cited like the other Old Testament books.
No. Chemnitz's answer to Trent says doctrine must be proved from the canonical books.

No, though they may support it. Article VI forbids applying them "to establish any doctrine." Yet the Homily of Alms Deeds uses Tobit 4 and 12:9 to teach that mercy and almsgiving "purgeth from all sins, and delivereth from death," explaining that this is by God's grace and not the worthiness of the works, which are the fruit of faith.

No, and it should not be used in the church except as a human writing (Westminster 1.3). Reformed writers point to teachings they think conflict with Scripture, such as alms that "cleanse away every sin" (12:9).
No. Wesley's Article V says Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation and names only the canonical books, so nothing can be required as doctrine from Tobit.
No. Doctrine rests on the 66 books listed in the London Baptist Confession (1.2), and the Apocrypha have no authority in the church (1.3).

canon.summary: Tobit is in the Old Testament of the Catholic Church and of the Eastern and Oriental Orthodox churches, including the Ethiopian; Catholics call it deuterocanonical. Lutherans and Anglicans place it among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches do not count it as Scripture, and it is not in the Jewish Bible.
accepted_by: Scripture, one of the deuterocanonical books. Augustine counted it in the canon (On Christian Teaching 2.8.13). It is on the list of the Council of Hippo (393), repeated at Carthage (397), and in Pope Innocent I's letter to Exsuperius (405), which names "one of Tobit" among the histories. The Council of Florence (1442), in its decree of union with the Copts, listed it. The Council of Trent (Session 4, 1546) defined the list, "Tobias" included, as sacred and canonical, the First Vatican Council (1870) confirmed Trent's list, and the Catechism (120) names Tobit among the books. For centuries the Catholic text was Jerome's Vulgate; most modern Catholic translations follow the longer Greek. Tobit is read at Mass, and Tobias and Sarah's prayer (8:4–8) is among the readings for weddings.

In the Old Testament, which the Orthodox read in the Greek of the Septuagint. Its exact rank has been explained in two ways. Athanasius (367) listed Tobit among books "to be read" by those preparing for baptism, not among the canonical books, and the Russian catechism of Philaret (1839) follows him. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672), answering Protestant ideas, named Tobit among the "genuine parts of Scripture." Kallistos Ware reports that most Orthodox scholars today treat these books as part of the Bible but on a lower footing than the rest; some Orthodox writers, as the Orthodox Church in America's answer does, simply call them canonical. Orthodox Bibles print it, and the church honors Raphael among the archangels (November 8).

In their Old Testament by long use, in Coptic, Syriac and Armenian translations made from the Greek. These churches never held a council like Trent to define the list, and their manuscripts and lectionaries vary in detail. A Coptic Orthodox diocese's teaching page says the deuterocanonical books were accepted by the Egyptian church and are found in the Coptic version in all its dialects. The Assyrian Church of the East is not covered here.
Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches
Scripture, among the Old Testament books of its 81-book Bible, in a Ge'ez translation made from the Greek. Cowley lists it in both the narrower and broader ways of counting the canon.

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles (Latin 1563, English 1571) names "the Book of Tobias" among the other books that, "as Hierome saith," the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not apply "to establish any doctrine." The King James Version (1611) printed it, the Prayer Book lectionary read it, and the 1662 Prayer Book used Tobit 4:7 and 4:8–9 among its offertory sentences. The Second Book of Homilies (1563), commended by Article XXXV, quotes Tobit in its Homily of Alms Deeds and explains its saying that alms purge sin as God's grace counting the merciful clean, with good works as the fruit of faith, not the cause of acceptance. Modern Anglican provinces differ in how much they read it.

Among the Apocrypha. Luther's complete Bible of 1534 gathered these books between the Testaments under a heading that called them books not held equal to Holy Scripture, yet useful and good to read. His preface to Tobit (1534) praised it as useful and good for Christians to read, whether it is history or a drama by a gifted poet. Lutheran confessions never fixed a canon; Martin Chemnitz (1565–73) taught that such books may not prove doctrine. Many Lutheran Bibles today leave them out.

Not Scripture. The Belgic Confession (1561) lets the church read the Apocrypha and take instruction from them as far as they agree with the canonical books, but not to confirm faith. The Westminster Confession (1646) says they are "no part of the canon of the Scripture" and are not "to be any otherwise approved, or made use of, than other human writings." Many Reformed Bibles printed them, with warnings, into the 1800s: the Dutch States Bible (1637), ordered by the Synod of Dort, did so, and the British and Foreign Bible Society stopped printing them only in 1827.

Not Scripture. The Global Anabaptist Mennonite Encyclopedia reports that Anabaptists followed the Reformers in denying the Apocrypha divine inspiration, while Menno Simons and Dirk Philips often cited them and books such as Tobit were highly esteemed. Old Order Amish weddings traditionally take the sermon from Tobit; a manuscript Amish ministers' manual calls it a book not counted among the books of Holy Scripture that "nevertheless gives a beautiful teaching."
Not Scripture. Wesley's Articles of Religion (1784) took over the Anglican list of canonical books but dropped the paragraph naming the Apocrypha.

Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) nearly repeats Westminster's words, calling the Apocrypha "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture." Most evangelical churches hold the 66 books and read Tobit, when they read it, as Jewish background to the New Testament, a view argued at length by Roger Beckwith and F. F. Bruce.

Not Scripture. Tobit is not in the Hebrew Bible. Origen reported (about 240) that the Jews did not use Tobit and did not have it even among their apocrypha in Hebrew, though the churches used it. Jews had copied it at Qumran, and in the Middle Ages Jewish writers retold it in Hebrew and Aramaic versions, It has never been part of the Jewish Bible, though one medieval Hebrew Tobit (Codex Or. Gaster 28) is headed "For the Second Day of Shavuot," which suggests some medieval communities read it on that feast.
Read and copied: four Aramaic copies and one Hebrew copy, published by Fitzmyer. Whether they counted it as Scripture is unknown, since there was no closed list yet.

Widely used and usually treated as Scripture, with some doubts. Polycarp (about 110–135) repeats its saying that alms rescue from death, 2 Clement echoes it, and Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 2.23; 6.12), Origen, Cyprian and Ambrose quote it, often as Scripture. Writers who followed the Hebrew count placed it lower, each in his own way: Athanasius (367) among books "appointed by the Fathers to be read" by those newly joining the church; Rufinus (about 404) among the "ecclesiastical" books read in church but not used to confirm faith; Jerome among books the church reads for the building up of the people; Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) gave those preparing for baptism a 22-book list without Tobit and told them to read only those. The North African councils, Innocent I and Augustine counted it in the canon.

provenance.h: When and where it was written
provenance.b: Most scholars date Tobit to about 225–175 BC (Fitzmyer), some as early as 300 BC. The reasons: the oldest Qumran copy is from about 100 BC, and the text had already been copied and changed before then; the book knows the Prophets as a collection (14:4–5) and seems to know the story of Ahiqar; it hopes for a rebuilt Temple but shows no sign of the crisis under Antiochus IV and the Maccabean revolt (167–164 BC). Where it was written is unknown. The eastern exile, Judea and Egypt have all been proposed, and none has won agreement.

provenance.h: The original language and the Qumran copies
provenance.b: Before the Dead Sea Scrolls, Tobit was known only in Greek and later translations, and scholars argued about whether it was first written in Greek, Hebrew or Aramaic. Cave 4 at Qumran settled part of the question. It yielded five fragmentary copies, published by Joseph Fitzmyer in 1995 (DJD 19): four in Aramaic (4Q196, a papyrus, and 4Q197, 4Q198, 4Q199) and one in Hebrew (4Q200). As Fitzmyer dates them, they were copied between about 100 BC and the early first century AD. They show that the book was written in a Semitic language, not Greek. Most scholars think Aramaic came first and the Hebrew is a translation, because the Aramaic copies are more numerous and older; a few think the Hebrew may be original. Where the fragments overlap the Greek, they agree with the longer form in Codex Sinaiticus.

• GII, the longer form, in Codex Sinaiticus (300s AD), which has two long gaps (4:7–19 and 13:6–10) and lacks a few single verses. Most scholars think it is closest to the original. The Plain English Translation follows it.
  • GI, the shorter form, in Codex Vaticanus (300s) and Codex Alexandrinus (400s) and most later manuscripts. It is smoother and briefer, probably a revision of a text like GII. The King James Version and most older translations follow it.
  • GIII, a third form found only in minuscules 106 and 107, and only for 6:9–12:22; for the rest of the book those manuscripts have the shorter text (Di Lella in NETS, following Hanhart).

Robert Hanhart's Göttingen edition (1983) prints GI and GII in full, one above the other. Swete's edition, used for this site, prints both Vaticanus and Sinaiticus.

The Old Latin (Vetus Latina), made in the 100s–300s AD, was translated from a Greek text close to GII, so scholars use it to fill the gaps in Sinaiticus, as Fitzmyer and Moore do. Several Old Latin manuscripts survive, and they differ among themselves.

Jerome's Vulgate is a different kind of text. In his preface, addressed to the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus, Jerome says that the Hebrews exclude the book from their divine Scriptures, that he was willing to face "the opinion of the Pharisees" to obey the bishops, and that he found a man skilled in both Hebrew and Aramaic and "took to the work of one day": the man put the Aramaic into Hebrew aloud, and Jerome dictated it in Latin to a scribe. The result is freer and shorter than the Greek, with its own additions: the three nights of prayer before the marriage is consummated (Vulgate 6:16–22; 8:4–5), the dog that runs ahead wagging its tail (11:9), and a reworded law of love, "see that you never do to another what you would hate to have done to you by another" (Vulgate 4:16, as the Douay-Rheims has it). The Vulgate, and the Douay-Rheims made from it, were the Catholic Tobit for over a thousand years.

• Syriac, Coptic, Armenian and Ethiopic translations were made from the Greek, mostly from the shorter form.
  • Medieval Hebrew and Aramaic versions. Several Jewish retellings survive, among them a Hebrew text printed in Constantinople in 1516 and edited by Sebastian Münster (1542), another edited by Paul Fagius (1542), and an Aramaic text from a Bodleian manuscript published by Adolf Neubauer (1878). Scholars think these are late versions made from Greek or Latin, not the original that Jerome or Qumran knew. Weeks, Gathercole and Stuckenbruck print the main versions side by side.

provenance.h: Ahiqar and the folk stories behind it
provenance.b:
The book weaves in a famous tale. The Story of Ahiqar, known from an Aramaic papyrus found at Elephantine in Egypt and copied in the 400s BC, tells of a wise official of the Assyrian kings Sennacherib and Esarhaddon who adopted his nephew Nadin (Nadab), and was betrayed by him and condemned to death. The papyrus breaks off before the end; later Syriac, Armenian and Arabic versions tell how Ahiqar was hidden, restored to the king's favor, and how Nadin was punished (Lindenberger). Tobit makes Ahiqar Tobit's own nephew (1:21–22), has him care for the blind Tobit (2:10), come with Nadab to share his joy at the homecoming (11:18), and recalls his betrayal as a lesson about alms (14:10). The writer clearly expected readers to know the story.

Scholars have also compared Tobit with widespread folk tales: "the grateful dead," in which a man who buries an unburied corpse is rewarded by a helper who turns out to be the dead man's spirit, and "the monster in the bridal chamber," in which a bride's husbands die until a hero is told how to defeat the creature. Tobit changes both: the helper is God's angel, and the remedy works through prayer.

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b:
Tobit is full of the books of the Hebrew Bible, and these links run from the Hebrew Bible to Tobit, not the other way.

  • Genesis 24 and Genesis 29: a son sent to kinsfolk in the east to find a wife, a meeting arranged by God, a welcome at the family's house.
  • Genesis 2:18: quoted in Tobias's prayer (8:6).
  • Amos 8:10: quoted by Tobit at the ruined feast (2:6).
  • Numbers 36:6–9 and the patriarchs' marriages: the ground for Tobit's teaching on marrying within the family (4:12; 6:12–13; 7:10–12).
  • Deuteronomy on the tithe and the poor (1:6–8; 4:7–11), on wages paid the same day (4:14; Deuteronomy 24:14–15).
  • Job 1–2: a righteous man struck down and mocked by his wife (2:11–14).
  • Jonah and Nahum: named as prophets of Nineveh's fall (14:4; the shorter Greek has Jonah, the longer Nahum).
  • Isaiah 54:11–12 and Isaiah 60: the Jerusalem of jewels to which the nations bring gifts (13:11–17).
  • Judges 13:20: the angel who goes up after revealing himself (12:20–21).

provenance.h: How Jews and Christians first used it
provenance.b: Apart from Qumran, Jewish writers of the time do not quote Tobit, though its teaching on alms is close to Sirach (Sirach 3:30; Sirach 29:12) and Daniel (Daniel 4:27). The negative form of the Golden Rule in 4:15, "Do not do to anyone what you hate," is close to the saying the Talmud gives to Hillel (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 31a) and to the Didache's "whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to another" (Didache 1.2). Christian use begins with Polycarp (To the Philippians 10.2), who repeats the line that alms rescue from death, and 2 Clement 16.4, which says almsgiving lightens sin.

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: Judaism's Bible has 24 books (the Christian Old Testament's 39 counted differently), and Tobit is not among them. Josephus, writing about AD 95, says the Jews have 22 books that were written from Moses to the reign of Artaxerxes, after which the exact line of prophets failed (Against Apion 1.38–41). Tobit, though set earlier, was written later. Origen reported that the Jews did not use Tobit and did not have it even among their apocrypha in Hebrew (Letter to Africanus). Protestants, and some Orthodox and earlier Catholic teachers, argue in its strongest form: the Old Testament was entrusted to Israel (Romans 3:2), Jesus and the apostles used Israel's Scriptures, and the New Testament never quotes Tobit as Scripture. So the church should receive the books Israel received. The Orthodox catechism of Philaret uses the same argument, though the Orthodox still read Tobit in church.

Jerome (about 347–420), the greatest biblical scholar of the early Latin church, made his Old Testament from the Hebrew, the Hebraica veritas, "Hebrew truth." In the preface to Samuel and Kings (about 391) he wrote that whatever is outside the Hebrew books is to be set among the apocrypha, and he named Tobit among them. In the preface to the books of Solomon he said the church reads Judith, Tobit and the Maccabees but does not receive them among the canonical Scriptures, reading them for the building up of the people, not to confirm church doctrine. That sentence is the source of Article VI. Yet Jerome translated Tobit at the bishops' request, and his preface shows he knew most churches used it. Athanasius and Rufinus drew a similar line, and Cyril of Jerusalem gave a 22-book list without Tobit. Augustine, by contrast, counted Tobit in the canon (On Christian Teaching 2.8.13), and the North African councils followed him. Even on the eve of Trent, Cardinal Cajetan (in a commentary of the early 1530s) followed Jerome's distinction, as Metzger reports.

Protestant writers from the 1500s on gave reasons from the book's content, in their strongest form:

  • Alms that purge sin. Raphael says alms rescue from death and "cleanse away every sin" (12:9; also 4:10). To readers of Paul, that seemed to make a human work the cause of forgiveness, against justification by grace through faith (Romans 3:24–28; Ephesians 2:8–9) and cleansing by Christ's blood (1 John 1:7).
  • An angel who presents prayers. Raphael says he brought the record of their prayers before God (12:12), and the shorter Greek calls the seven angels those who "present the prayers of the saints" (12:15, shorter Greek). The Reformers saw this used to support the intercession of angels and saints, against the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).
  • Remedies that look like magic. Smoke from a fish's heart and liver drives off a demon, and its gall cures blindness (6:7–9; 8:2–3; 11:11–13). Archibald Alexander (1826) called the story "fabulous," and others compared it with charms forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10–12.
  • An angel who gives a false name. Raphael says, "I am Azariah, son of the great Hananiah, one of your kinsmen" (5:13), which Protestant writers called a plain falsehood unworthy of a holy angel.
  • Food on the graves. "Pour out your bread on the grave of the righteous" (4:17, from the shorter Greek) was read as support for offerings for the dead.

Westminster's conclusion (1.3) follows: not inspired, no authority, to be used no otherwise than other human writings. Not every Protestant church read the alms texts this way: the Church of England's Homily of Alms Deeds quotes Tobit and explains that alms "purgeth from all sins" because God by his grace reckons the merciful clean, not because of the worthiness of the works.

Scholars of every church note that the book's history and geography do not fit what is known of the Assyrian period: Tobit lives from the division of the kingdom (about 930 BC) to the fall of Nineveh (612 BC); Sennacherib is called Shalmaneser's son; the Galilee deportation is put under the wrong king; Rages is placed two days from Ecbatana. These are set out under "How reliable is it?" For Protestants they confirm that the book is not inspired history. For most Catholic and Orthodox scholars they show what kind of book it is, a story told to teach, which says nothing against its inspiration.

rejected_why.h: How the churches that keep it answer
rejected_why.b: Catholic and Orthodox teachers answer each point. On the canon: both say the church received the Old Testament in Greek from the apostles' time, the Septuagint that the New Testament writers often quote, and has read Tobit since the early centuries: Polycarp already repeats its saying on alms, and Cyprian and Augustine cite it as Scripture. Catholic teachers add that the canon was the church's to recognize, as Hippo, Carthage, Innocent I, Florence and Trent did. Orthodox teachers do not appeal to Florence or Trent, which the East did not receive; they point to the Septuagint the church has always read, to the Council in Trullo (692), which received the canons of Carthage, and to the Synod of Jerusalem (1672). On alms: the Hebrew Bible itself says sin is atoned for by loyal love and faithfulness (Proverbs 16:6) and tells a king to break off his sins by righteousness, which the Greek renders "alms" (Daniel 4:27); Jesus says to give alms and all will be clean (Luke 11:41); love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). Alms done in grace show and deepen repentance; they do not replace Christ. On angels: Revelation 8:3–4 shows an angel offering the prayers of the saints. On the remedies: God heals through means, as with Isaiah's fig cake (2 Kings 20:7) or Jesus' mud (John 9:6), and the book credits God, not the fish (11:14–15; 12:14). On the false name: Walter Drum (1912) and others note that "Azariah son of Hananiah" means "the LORD helps, son of the LORD is gracious," a true description of the angel's mission, as the end of the story reveals.

cited_in.b: Jesus' Golden Rule, do to others what you want them to do to you (also Luke 6:31), is the positive form of Tobit's "Do not do to anyone what you hate" (4:15, translated from the shorter Greek, since Sinaiticus has a gap here). The negative form was a common Jewish and Greek saying: Hillel's summary of the Torah (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 31a) is close to Tobit's, and the Didache (1.2) uses the same negative form. Tobit is the oldest Jewish witness to it, but Jesus' words need not depend on Tobit.

The seven angels who stand before God, and an angel who offers incense with the prayers of the saints. Raphael is "one of the seven angels" who stand before the Lord's glory (12:15), and the shorter Greek calls them angels who "present the prayers of the saints" (12:15, shorter Greek); he brought the record of Tobit's and Sarah's prayers before God (12:12). Many commentators think Revelation knows this tradition, perhaps from Tobit. The seven angels also appear in 1 Enoch 20 and grow from Ezekiel 9:2, so this is a probable allusion in many commentators' view, but direct use of Tobit is not proven.

"I am Gabriel, the one who stands before God" (literally from the Greek): the angel's self-introduction is very like Raphael's, "I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand" before the Lord (12:15). Both angels reveal their names after being doubted or unrecognized. Commentators often compare the two; most see a shared Jewish way of speaking of the angels of the presence rather than a quotation.

The angel tells Cornelius, a man known for his alms and prayers, that they "have gone up as a memorial before God." Raphael says he brought the "memorial" (Greek mnēmosynon, the same word) of Tobit's prayer before the Lord's glory, and that he was sent when Tobit buried the dead (12:12–14). The pairing of prayer and alms remembered in heaven is close. Probably shared tradition, possibly an echo; disputed.

The Sadducees' riddle about a woman married in turn to seven brothers, who all died childless (also Matthew 22:23–33; Luke 20:27–38). Sarah had seven husbands who all died (3:8; 6:14), and her marriage to Tobias is arranged as a family right (6:12–13; 7:10–11). Some scholars think the Sadducees, who rejected the resurrection and probably books like Tobit, mocked a story their opponents loved. Others think the riddle simply builds on the law of Deuteronomy 25:5–10. Possible, unproven.

Jesus teaches on almsgiving, prayer and fasting together, done for God and not to be seen. Tobit 12:8 joins the same three in the shorter Greek (prayer with fasting and alms; the longer Greek has prayer and alms only), and the whole book shows alms and prayer remembered by God (12:12–14). Many commentators see Tobit as the closest Jewish background to this triad; a direct literary link is not claimed, and the shared Jewish practice may explain both.

Grace from the seven spirits before God's throne (also Revelation 4:5). Some commentators link these to the seven angels of the presence, of whom Raphael is one (12:15); others read the seven spirits as the Holy Spirit in his fullness (Isaiah 11:2; Zechariah 4:2–10). Disputed in meaning, so the link to Tobit is uncertain.

Golden bowls of incense, which are the prayers of the saints, held before the Lamb. Raphael carries the memorial of prayer before God's glory (12:12), and in the shorter Greek the seven angels present the prayers of the saints (12:15). Shared picture of heavenly beings who bring prayer before God; see also Revelation 8:3–4.

The little ones' angels always see the face of the Father in heaven. Catholic and Orthodox writers often join this verse to Raphael's guarding of Tobias as the basis of teaching on guardian angels; Raphael stands in attendance before God's glory (12:15) and is sent to guide and protect (5:4; 12:14). Shared tradition.

Each should take a wife in holiness and honor, not in lustful passion like the Gentiles. Tobias says he takes Sarah not for sexual immorality but in truth (8:7). A shared Jewish ideal of marriage set against pagan custom; no direct link is claimed.

To the King of the ages be honor and glory. Tobit's hymn twice calls God "the King of the ages" (13:6; 13:10). A Jewish title of God used in prayer; Tobit is one early witness to it, not a source of 1 Timothy.

Jesus praises the Father as Lord of heaven and earth (also Luke 10:21). In the shorter Greek of 7:17 Edna blesses Sarah in the name of "the Lord of heaven and earth"; the longer Greek, which the Plain English Translation follows, has "the Lord of heaven" only. A common Jewish form of address (Genesis 14:19); no dependence.

When you give a feast, invite the poor. At his Pentecost meal Tobit sends his son to find a poor kinsman to share it (2:2). A shared Jewish practice of feeding the poor at feasts (Deuteronomy 16:11; Nehemiah 8:10); no direct link.

Each should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly, for God loves a cheerful giver. Tobit says not to give alms with a grudging eye (4:7; 4:16), an idiom from Deuteronomy 15:9–10. Shared tradition.

Jesus tells the Pharisees to give alms from what is inside, and everything will be clean for them. Tobit says alms "cleanse away every sin" (12:9). Catholic and Orthodox teachers read the two together; Protestant teachers read Luke's saying as a rebuke of outward religion, not a means of forgiveness. Shared tradition of alms and cleansing; no direct link is claimed.

The new Jerusalem with walls of jasper, foundations of precious stones, gates of pearl and a street of gold. Tobit's Jerusalem has gates of sapphire and emerald, walls of precious stone, towers of gold and streets set with red gems and stone of Ophir (13:16–17). Both build on Isaiah 54:11–12, so this is a shared hope rather than a borrowing, though Tobit is the closest Jewish parallel before Revelation.

Store up treasure in heaven, not on earth (also Luke 12:33; 1 Timothy 6:18–19). Tobit tells his son that by giving alms he puts away a good deposit for the day of need (4:9, shorter Greek; compare 12:8); the Greek verb is thēsaurizeis, "you store up treasure," the same root as Matthew's. The idea of alms as treasure with God is common to Tobit, Sirach 29:11–12 and Jesus' teaching. Shared tradition; no one claims a quotation.

The works by which the nations are judged: feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, caring for strangers and prisoners. Tobit lists his own works in the same terms, bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked (1:17; 4:16), and adds burying the dead (1:17–18). Christian tradition later joined the two lists into the seven corporal works of mercy, with burying the dead from Tobit. Shared Jewish tradition; not a quotation.

Love covers a great number of sins (from Proverbs 10:12; compare James 5:20). Tobit says alms rescue from death and "cleanse away every sin" (12:9). Both belong to a Jewish tradition in which deeds of mercy deal with sin (Proverbs 16:6; Daniel 4:27; Sirach 3:30), which 2 Clement 16.4 joins to Tobit's words. How the two should be related is one of the points on which the churches disagree (see the card "Where Christians differ").

Some have entertained angels without knowing it. Commentators usually think first of Abraham (Genesis 18) and Lot (Genesis 19), but Tobit's family, who host Raphael for weeks without knowing him (5:4–6:1; 12:1–5), is the fullest Jewish example. Shared tradition; a specific link to Tobit is possible but unprovable.

The angel who forbids John to worship him: "I am a servant with you... Worship God!" (Revelation 19:10; also Revelation 22:8–9). When Tobit and Tobias fall down in fear, Raphael tells them he came not by his own favor but by God's will, and that they should bless God (12:16–18). Both reflect the Jewish concern that angels not be worshiped. Shared tradition.

A traveler walks with disciples who do not recognize him, reveals himself at a meal and vanishes, and then the risen Jesus eats fish to show he is not a spirit. Raphael travels unrecognized, reveals himself after a meal, says he only seemed to eat (12:19), and goes up to God (12:20). Some commentators compare the stories; most see no direct link. Disputed.
Jesus says he is going to the one who sent him. Raphael says the same of himself before he ascends (12:20). A similar phrase, natural for any messenger who returns; few see dependence.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Jewish faith and family life in the 200s BC, Tobit is very valuable: the Qumran copies prove it was read before Jesus, and it shows prayer, fasting, alms, burial of the dead, marriage customs, angels and demons as many Jews knew them. As a text, it survived well in substance but in more than one form: two main Greek versions that differ in hundreds of places, an Old Latin, Jerome's free Vulgate, and Semitic fragments that cover only part of the book. As history, its setting in Assyria in the 700s BC does not fit the known record: the chronology, the order of the kings and the geography are wrong in ways a writer living there would not have made. Most scholars, including most Catholic scholars since the mid-1900s, read it as a story told to teach. Catholic teaching on literary forms (Divino Afflante Spiritu; Dei Verbum 12) leaves room for that, and the Church has made no ruling on Tobit's genre, while older Catholic and some Orthodox readers defend its history. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees with their core faith and ethics, goes beyond them on angels and demons, and in its teaching on alms and its picture of angels it touches points where the churches disagree.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish faith before Jesus: very high
sections.b: Here no church disagrees. The Qumran copies show the book was being read by about 100 BC, in both Aramaic and Hebrew. It gives one of the fullest pictures we have of ordinary Jewish piety in the centuries before Jesus: prayers are offered in distress, at journeys and at a wedding; tithes are given in Jerusalem (1:6–8); the dead are buried at once; the poor are fed; wages are paid the same day; marriage is arranged within the family with a written contract (7:13); and food laws are kept among Gentiles (1:10–11). It also shows beliefs the New Testament assumes: angels who guard, guide and carry prayers to God, named angels, seven angels of the presence, demons who harm people, and hope for the ingathering of Israel and the nations. Its almsgiving teaching helps explain why alms and prayer go together in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:1–18) and in Acts 10.

Good in substance, uncertain in detail. The story and its teaching are the same in every version. But the two Greek forms differ in hundreds of places, the longer one (Sinaiticus) has two gaps, and the Qumran fragments, though they confirm that the longer form is closer to the original, cover only parts of the book and are often broken. The Old Latin helps but its own manuscripts differ. Jerome's Vulgate is a free and hurried translation of an Aramaic copy we no longer have, and it changes many details. So for many verses the exact wording is uncertain, and the variant notes say so. Compared with most books of the Hebrew Bible, whose Hebrew text survives complete, the original-language text of Tobit is much less secure.

The book sets itself in Assyria from about 730 to 670 BC. The details do not fit what is known:

  • Chronology. Tobit says that when he was young his tribe broke away from Jerusalem and the house of David (1:4–5), which happened about 930 BC. He is taken captive under Shalmaneser (1:2), about 725 BC; in the longer Greek he dies at 112 (14:1; the shorter Greek gives 158 at 14:11) yet lives to hear of Nineveh's fall (14:15), in 612 BC. No single life can span 930 to 612 BC.
  • The kings. The book calls Sennacherib the son of Shalmaneser (1:15). He was the son of Sargon II, who is not mentioned. The Greek names Shalmaneser "Enemessar."
  • The deportation. Naphtali was taken by Tiglath-pileser III about 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29), not by Shalmaneser.
  • The timing of Sennacherib's death. The book has him killed by his sons within forty days (fifty in the shorter Greek) of his flight from Judea (1:18–21). He returned from Judea in 701 BC and was murdered in 681 BC (2 Kings 19:36–37).
  • The fall of Nineveh. The shorter Greek says Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus took it (14:15). It fell in 612 BC to the Babylonians under Nabopolassar and the Medes under Cyaxares; the longer Greek's "Achiacharus king of Media" may be a garbled form of Cyaxares.
  • Geography. Raphael says Rages is two days from Ecbatana, Rages in the mountains and Ecbatana in the plain (5:6, longer Greek). The real distance is about 300 km (some 190 miles), and Alexander the Great, marching hard in pursuit of Darius, took eleven days to cover it (Arrian, Anabasis 3.20), and commentators note that the description of mountain and plain is the reverse of the real ground.

The Catholic answer. Older Catholic scholars defended the history point by point: Walter Drum (1912) read Enemessar as Sargon, joined the deportations under several kings, and called the fall-of-Nineveh names copyists' errors. Since Pius XII's encyclical Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943), Catholic interpreters are urged to identify the literary forms the biblical writers used, and the Second Vatican Council's Dei Verbum (11–12) teaches that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted written for our salvation, and that truth is expressed differently in history, prophecy, poetry and other forms. On that basis most Catholic scholars today, such as Fitzmyer, read Tobit as a story told to teach, and see no conflict between that and its inspiration. The Orthodox answer. The Orthodox churches have made no ruling known to us on whether Tobit's events happened. They read the book in the church for its moral and spiritual teaching, and many Orthodox teachers, following Athanasius, already give these books a different rank from the Hebrew canon, so the historical questions weigh less. Some Orthodox and Catholic readers still take the events as history and explain the difficulties as copyists' errors or gaps in our knowledge. A fair summary: the evidence strongly favors a story written long after the events; whether that matters for its authority depends on what kind of book a church thinks it is.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: one God, creator and judge, who hears prayer (3:11–15; 8:5–8; 13:1–6); honor your father and mother (4:3–4; Exodus 20:12); care for the poor, the widow and the stranger, and fair wages paid on the day (4:7–16; Deuteronomy 24:14–15); marriage as God's gift from creation (8:6; Genesis 2:18); God disciplines and shows mercy (13:2; Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6); hope of the return of the exiles and of nations coming to Jerusalem (13:11; 14:5–7; Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 60).
  • Goes beyond: a named angel (Raphael) who travels for weeks in human form; seven angels of the presence (12:15); a named demon who kills from jealousy and is driven off and bound (3:8; 8:3); angels presenting the memory of prayers (12:12). The New Testament shares some of this (named Gabriel and Michael, seven angels before God in Revelation 8:2, angels who guard in Matthew 18:10 and Acts 12:15) and never mentions the rest. Marrying only within one's own tribe (4:12–13) is stricter than the Torah's general rule, which asks it only of heiresses (Numbers 36:6–9).
  • Differs or may conflict: (a) Alms that purge every sin (12:9; 4:10). Protestants see a conflict with justification by faith and forgiveness through Christ (Romans 3:24–28; Hebrews 9:22). Catholic and Orthodox teachers see agreement with Proverbs 16:6, Daniel 4:27, Luke 11:41 and 1 Peter 4:8: alms done in grace are a fruit and means of repentance. (b) Angels presenting prayers (12:12, 15): Protestants see it in tension with one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5); Catholics and Orthodox compare Revelation 8:3–4. (c) The fish remedies (6:7–9; 8:2–3; 11:11–13): some see them as close to forbidden charms (Deuteronomy 18:10–12); others see medicine that God blesses, with the cure credited to God. (d) The angel's assumed name (5:13): read as a lie by some Protestants, as a disguise with a true meaning by Catholic writers such as Drum. (e) Bread on the graves of the righteous (4:17): it may mean feeding mourners at a funeral, or offerings for the dead, which the Torah forbids from tithes (Deuteronomy 26:14). (f) The historical setting (section 3).
  • Each church's view: Catholic and Orthodox churches read Tobit as Scripture in harmony with the rest of the Bible and with the church's teaching, so they read (a) to (e) in the ways given above. Lutheran and Anglican churches read it as a good human book, useful for life, to be tested by the canonical books and never used to establish doctrine. Reformed, Baptist and most evangelical churches see points (a) to (d) as signs that the book is not inspired, while valuing it as a window on Jewish faith before Christ.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture. If you are Catholic or Orthodox, Tobit is in your Bible, and your church's teaching and worship are your guide to it. If you are Protestant, it is not Scripture for you, though Lutheran and Anglican tradition commends it for example of life, and every reader can learn from it how Jews lived and prayed before Christ. Either way, read it with respect and with an eye to the differences on this page.

Check the introduction of your Bible. Most modern Catholic, Orthodox and ecumenical Bibles translate the longer Greek (Sinaiticus); the King James Apocrypha and older Protestant Bibles translate the shorter Greek; the Douay-Rheims translates Jerome's Vulgate. A verse you remember may be missing, worded differently, or numbered differently in another Bible. The variant notes on this site point out the differences that matter.

how_to_read.h: Read it as a story with a message
how_to_read.b: Watch for the irony: from 5:4 the reader knows Azariah is Raphael, and the characters' worries and plans become gentle comedy. Watch for the double plot (Tobit and Sarah), the prayers at each turning point (3:1–6; 3:11–15; 8:5–8; 11:14–15; 13), and the speeches that state the lessons (4; 12:6–10; 14:3–11). Ask what each scene shows about how God works: quietly, through ordinary journeys, family ties and acts of mercy.

Read Genesis 24 before Tobit 5–7, Job 1–2 before Tobit 2–3, and Isaiah 60 before Tobit 13. Then read Matthew 6:1–18 and Acts 10 after Tobit 12. You will see how Tobit takes up the Hebrew Bible and how close its piety is to the world of the New Testament, and you can judge for yourself where it agrees, goes beyond, or differs.

On alms, angels, the fish and the angel's name, the churches give real answers, set out above and in the "Where Christians differ" cards. Read each in its strongest form before deciding. Many Protestant readers find that the book's teaching on alms sounds less strange once they read Proverbs 16:6, Daniel 4:27 and Luke 11:41; many Catholic readers find the Reformers' worries less strange once they see how the verses were used in the 1500s.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "Tobit, in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants." Say which text you quote (longer Greek, shorter Greek or Vulgate). It is one of the best backgrounds for angels in the Gospels and Acts, for almsgiving in the Sermon on the Mount, and for the Sadducees' question about seven husbands.
